newsitem.title: CHINA: China province to flatten graves for farmland.
newsitem.headline: China province to flatten graves for farmland.

text.p: Northern Chinese authorities have ordered nearly 10 million grave mounds to be levelled to boost the acreage of precious arable land, state media said on Monday.
Officials in Hebei province were urging local farmers to abandon traditional burials in favour of more economical and space-saving cremations, the Xinhua news agency said.
State protected sites such as ancient tombs, the graves of communist revolutionary heroes and celebrities and the ancestral sepulchre of overseas Chinese would be spared from the bulldozer, it said.
"Farmland occupied by grave mounds still remains a chronic issue in some areas," the China Daily said.
Hebei, a major grain and cotton producer, had 9.6 million graves taking up more than 21,330 hectares (52,700 acres) of otherwise good arable soil, the newspaper said.
Areas with barren hills unsuitable for farming would be allowed to set up public mass graveyards where the contents of of the former graves could be placed, it said.
"Burying the dead in the ground is still allowed in some rural areas but grave mounds on farmland are prohibited," the newspaper said.
An estimated 2.18 million bodies had been cremated by the end of 1995, saving some 2,400 hectares (5,900 acres) of farmland, the newspaper said.

Beijing has struggled to keep urban development, rural industry and erosion from encroaching on precious cropland, saying it must feed one-fifth of the world's population on just seven percent of its arable land.

The Financial News urged police and bank officials to crack down on people who burned stacks of bank notes as part of traditional funeral rites, saying the practice was superstitious and undermined the stability of the currency.

Many Chinese, defying numerous campaigns by communist rulers to stamp out such "feudal" practices, make offerings of money or food to deceased relatives in the belief that such sacrifices can assist the dead in the afterlife.
Superstition, virtually eliminated in the years after the communists came to power in 1949, has staged a comeback along with economic reforms.
